Hi team,

Following up with some concrete questions our engineers want answered before the next technical call. Apologies if some are basic — want to make sure we size correctly.

1) Chat vs Completions: For our assistant we'll have ongoing context + system prompts. When should we prefer the chat API vs a completions-style call for structured outputs (JSON) and streaming?

2) Tokenization / max_tokens: We need guidelines to compute max_tokens for both response and cost-estimates. If we have a 2k-token context and want up to a ~500-token response, any tips on padding, truncation, and counting?

3) Stop sequences: We plan to enforce a strict JSON output schema. Are stop sequences reliable across interrupted streaming? Best practices?

4) Streaming semantics: If we stream partial tokens to the client while also emitting an intermediate function/tool call (e.g., model decides to call a DB lookup mid-response), how is that represented? Can we stream until the function call is invoked and then switch to a tool payload?

5) Embeddings / reranker: For reranking search hits, do you recommend pre-computing embeddings server-side and using Redwood's embedding endpoint, or running an on-host nearest-neighbor locally? Pros/cons for latency and freshness.

Thanks — we'll collect a sample payload and sample index size to share.

Best,
Sara

From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Follow-up - request/response schema questions

Hi Sara / Alex — thanks for the clear list. Answers inline, plus a short example of how we recommend wiring the SDK for streaming + function calls.

1) Chat vs Completions - Prefer the chat API when you maintain conversational state, need system/user/assistant role separation, or will use function/tool calls. The chat API supports structured function calls natively and preserves role metadata. Use completions for single-shot prompts where you control the entire prompt string and don't need role tracking. For strict JSON output and function calling, chat is the better default.

2) Tokenization / max_tokens - Count tokens using the same tokenizer the model uses (we provide a token-counting util in the SDK). For cost and latency budgeting: total_tokens = prompt_tokens + response_max_tokens. If you expect 2k context and want up to 500 response, set response max_tokens=520 as a small buffer. For streaming latency, prefer lower max_tokens and early-stopping policies; set a hard ceiling to prevent runaway costs. Also consider prefix caching for repeated system text to reduce prompt_tokens seen by the runtime.

3) Stop sequences / strict JSON - Stop sequences are helpful but not guaranteed in every edge case (models can still output stray tokens). For robust enforcement, we recommend function-call mode with structured outputs (i.e., define a function signature that emits typed fields) or post-parse validation with a small deterministic cleanup pass. If you must use stop sequences, keep them unique and token-safe (e.g., <|end_json|>). In streaming, a stop token will terminate the token stream from the model; you should still validate the resulting payload once the stream completes.

4) Streaming + function/tool calls - Our SDK supports token streaming and in-stream function invocation markers. Recommended pattern:

- Start chat streaming to client.
- At inference time the model can emit a function_call event (separate event type in the stream) indicating name and arguments; the SDK will surface that event to your application before the full response completes.
- Application can pause streaming, execute the tool (DB lookup), then resume by sending the function result back to the model as the next message and continue streaming the subsequent tokens.

This lets you keep low latency for tokens up to the function call, handle the tool invocation, and then stream the updated continuation. Latency impact: you pay the RTT for the tool call and the extra model turn; design can minimize this by keeping tool executions fast or pre-fetching likely candidates.

Example (pseudo-Rust / JS snippet inline):

const stream = client.chat.stream({ model: 'redwood-rt-medium', messages, stream: true, max_tokens: 500 });
stream.on('token', t => sendToClient(t));
stream.on('function_call', fc => {
  // fc = { name: 'lookup_customer', arguments: '{"id":"123"}' }
  const toolResult = callDB(JSON.parse(fc.arguments));
  client.chat.send({ role: 'tool', name: fc.name, content: JSON.stringify(toolResult) });
});

(We can provide a full repo sample in the Drive if helpful.)

5) Embeddings + reranker - Trade-offs:
- Pre-compute embeddings server-side + store in a vector DB: best for low latency at query time and consistent scoring; needs batch re-ingest for freshness.
- On-host nearest-neighbor (local index): good for single-tenant deployments where data cannot leave your VPC; can be very low latency if you pin a memory-mapped index on the same hosts.

Recommendation: for Acme's search reranker, start with pre-computed embeddings in a hosted vector DB (gives fastest time-to-value). If you need sub-10ms tail latency or strict data residency, we can propose a Dedicated/private setup with a local index and Redwood routing to a private endpoint.

If useful, we can run a short perf experiment against a 1M-document sample to quantify P99 latencies and token costs.

Action items from us:
- Share SDK quickstart repo link in Drive (I'll upload the full sample with auth snippets).
- Put a short doc explaining how the streaming/function events map to the client and a sample JSON schema for function outputs.

I'll upload those by EOD. Happy to sync on a technical call after you share the sample payload.

Thanks,
